title: 〜に〜をあげる・くれる・もらう (giving and receiving things)
meaning: Express giving and receiving things. Choose 「あげる」, 「くれる」, or 「もらう」 depending on who gives to whom.
connection: A は B に noun を あげる／A が (私に) noun を くれる／A は B に (から) noun を もらう

senses.label: Giving to others
senses.meaning: 「あげる」 means “I (or my side) give to someone else”, or “a third person gives to another third person”. The direction is outward from the speaker's side. It cannot be used when someone gives something to me.
senses.connection: A は B に noun を あげる (あげます／あげた)
examples: I gave my mother flowers on Mother's Day.
Tanaka gave Yamada some chocolate.
You can have this book.

senses.label: Someone gives to me
senses.meaning: 「くれる」 means “someone gives to me (or to someone on my side)”. The direction is inward, toward the speaker. When the receiver is “me”, 「私に」 is usually left out.
senses.connection: A が (私に) noun を くれる (くれます／くれた)
examples: A friend gave me a birthday present.
My older sister gave my younger sister some sweets. (told from the younger sister's side)
My dad doesn't give me any pocket money.

senses.label: Receiving from others
senses.meaning: 「もらう」 takes the receiver as the subject: “get something from someone”. The giver is marked with 「に」 or 「から」. It works both for “I received” and for “a third person received”.
senses.connection: A は B に／B から noun を もらう (もらいます／もらった)
examples: I got a dictionary from an older student.
I got a bonus from the company.
My little brother got a watch from his grandfather.

notes: It's all about direction. When someone gives to me, only 「くれる」 works: ✕「友達が私にプレゼントをあげた」.
The same event can be said two ways: 「友達がくれた」＝「友達にもらった」. The first takes the giver as subject, the second the receiver.
When the giver is an organization such as a company or school, 「もらう」 usually takes 「から」, not 「に」.
Toward superiors, use the honorific forms 「さしあげる・くださる・いただく」. Toward people below you or animals, 「やる」 is possible.

daily.title: Talking about gifts with a friend
daily.description: Friends chatting about what they got for their birthday.
daily.example: What did your boyfriend give you?

daily.title: Giving away something extra
daily.description: Casually giving a friend something you don't need.
daily.example: I've got two of these pens, so here's one for you.

daily.title: Thanking family
daily.description: A child talks about pocket money from Grandma.
daily.example: Grandma gave me New Year's money!

work.title: Sharing souvenirs with coworkers
work.description: Handing out snacks after a business trip. Plain forms are fine between coworkers.
work.example: Is it OK if I give everyone the souvenirs from my business trip?

work.title: Explaining where materials came from
work.description: Telling a coworker where you got a document.
work.example: I got these materials from the sales department.

etymology: 「あげる」 originally meant “to raise, lift up” (上げる); from “offering upward” it came to mean “give”. 「くれる」 comes from the old verb 「くる (呉る)」, which already meant “give (to someone below)”. 「もらう」 originally meant “to ask for and receive”. In modern Japanese these giving/receiving verbs are usually written in kana.

similar.title: 〜てあげる・〜てくれる・〜てもらう
similar.explanation: Attached to a verb te-form, what is given is not a thing but an action or favor. The direction rules are the same as here.

similar.title: さしあげる・くださる・いただく
similar.explanation: The honorific versions of 「あげる」, 「くれる」, and 「もらう」. Use them when the giver or receiver is a superior, an elder, or a client.

similar.title: 渡す
similar.explanation: 「渡す」 just means “hand over, pass”. It has no sense of giving a gift or doing a favor. For handing over documents or keys, 「渡す」 is the usual verb.

title: 〜さしあげる・いただく・くださる (honorific giving and receiving)
meaning: Honorific ways to give and receive things: 「さしあげる」 for giving to a superior, 「くださる」 when a superior gives to me, and 「いただく」 for receiving from a superior.
connection: B に noun を さしあげる／A が noun を くださる／A に (から) noun を いただく

senses.label: Giving to a superior
senses.meaning: 「さしあげる」 is the humble form of 「あげる」. My side gives something to a superior, an elder, or a guest. It raises the receiver.
senses.connection: (私は) 目上の人に noun を さしあげる (差し上げる)
examples: I presented my teacher with a bouquet.
We are giving a commemorative gift to customers who visit our store.

senses.label: A superior gives to me
senses.meaning: 「くださる」 is the respectful form of 「くれる」. A superior or elder gives something to me (or my side). It raises the giver. The masu-form is 「くださいます」.
senses.connection: 目上の人が (私に) noun を くださる (くださいます／くださった)
examples: The company president gave us some souvenirs.
My teacher gave me a dictionary.

senses.label: Receiving from a superior
senses.meaning: 「いただく」 is the humble form of 「もらう」. With my side as subject, it means receiving something from a superior. It is also the humble way to say “eat” or “drink”.
senses.connection: (私は) 目上の人に／から noun を いただく (頂く)
examples: I received a congratulatory gift from the department manager.
I received a letter from my teacher.
We received valuable feedback from our customers.

notes: The masu-form of 「くださる」 is 「くださいます」, not ✕「くださります」.
Saying 「さしあげる」 directly to the superior can sound pushy. Face to face, people usually say 「どうぞ」 or 「お持ちください」 instead.
As auxiliary verbs, 「いただく」 and 「くださる」 are usually written in kana. As main verbs, 「頂く」 and 「下さる」 are also possible.

daily.title: Thanking a teacher
daily.description: A student talks about something the teacher gave them.
daily.example: The book you gave me has been really useful.

daily.title: Guests at home
daily.description: The host mentions something an elderly neighbor gave them.
daily.example: The elderly lady next door gave us some vegetables.

work.title: A thank-you business email
work.description: Writing to thank a client for a gift.
work.example: Thank you very much for the wonderful gift.

work.title: Announcing a store promotion
work.description: A clerk explains a free gift to customers.
work.example: We are giving free samples to customers who make a purchase.

etymology: 「さしあげる」 is the prefix 「差し」 (for emphasis) + 「上げる」, meaning “to hold up with both hands and offer”. 「いただく」 originally meant “to put on top of one's head” (頂く); people once raised gifts from superiors above their heads out of respect, which led to the meaning “receive”. 「くださる」 comes from the respectful form of 「下す」, meaning “to bestow (from above)”.

similar.title: あげる・くれる・もらう
similar.explanation: The plain forms, used among equals, family, and friends. With superiors or in formal situations, switch to the honorific forms in this entry.

similar.title: 〜ていただく
similar.explanation: Attached to a verb te-form, what you receive is the other person's action, not a thing. 「先生に本をいただいた」 is receiving a book; 「先生に本を貸していただいた」 is having the teacher kindly lend you a book.

similar.title: 〜てくださる
similar.explanation: Also an auxiliary use: a superior does something for me.

meaning: The humble form of 「〜てもらう」. It means having a superior or someone else do something for me, with a feeling of gratitude.
connection: Verb te-form + いただく (いただきます／いただいた)

senses.label: Receiving a kindness
senses.meaning: With my side as subject, it means receiving a favor in the form of an action from a superior. It carries thanks. The person who does the action is marked with 「に」.
senses.connection: 目上の人に verb te-form + いただく／いただいた
examples: My teacher kindly corrected my essay.
The department manager kindly drove me to the station.
Thank you for taking the time to come despite your busy schedule.

senses.label: Asking someone to do
senses.meaning: Used to state a request or rule for the listener. Softer and more polite than a direct command. Common in service, announcements, and business.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + いただきます／いただくことになります／いただけますか
examples: Please write your name here.
I'd like you to read the materials before the meeting.
Could you wait a moment, please?

notes: The doer is marked with 「に」: 「先生に教えていただく」. You cannot say ✕「先生が教えていただく」; with 「が」, use 「先生が教えてくださる」.
「お／ご + masu-stem / kanji noun + いただく」 is even more formal, as in 「お待ちいただく」 and 「ご確認いただく」.
「〜させていただく」 means “please let me do”; see 「〜させてください・〜させてもらう」.

daily.title: Thanking a teacher
daily.description: A student expresses thanks to a teacher.
daily.example: You wrote me a letter of recommendation, and it really helped. Thank you.

daily.title: Thanking an older neighbor
daily.description: Thanking a neighbor for looking after your child.
daily.example: Thank you so much for watching my child yesterday.

work.title: A request in a business email
work.description: Politely asking someone to check something by email.
work.example: I would appreciate it if you could check the attached file.

work.title: Paperwork at a counter
work.description: A staff member explains a procedure to a visitor.
work.example: Please fill out this form.

work.title: Opening a meeting
work.description: The host thanks everyone for attending.
work.example: Thank you very much for gathering here today.

etymology: 「いただく」 originally meant “to put on top of one's head” (頂く). People once raised gifts from superiors above their heads out of respect, so it became the humble form of 「もらう」. After a te-form, what is received expanded from things to actions and favors.

similar.title: 〜てもらう
similar.explanation: The plain form, used with friends and family. 「〜ていただく」 is its humble form, for superiors, clients, and formal situations.

similar.title: 〜てくださる
similar.explanation: Two ways to describe the same event: 「先生が教えてくださった」 takes the teacher as subject and raises the teacher; 「先生に教えていただいた」 takes me as subject and lowers me.

similar.title: 〜ていただけませんか
similar.explanation: The negative question of the potential form of 「いただく」. It is used only for polite requests and is more polite than 「〜ていただけますか」.

meaning: The respectful form of 「〜てくれる」. A superior or someone else does something for me (or my side). It raises the doer and expresses gratitude.
connection: Verb te-form + くださる (くださいます／くださった)

senses.label: A superior does it for me
senses.meaning: With the doer as subject, it means a superior, elder, or client did something for my side. It raises the other person and carries gratitude.
senses.connection: 目上の人が verb te-form + くださる／くださいました
examples: My teacher explained it to me carefully.
The company president came all the way to the station to pick me up.
It's all thanks to everyone's support.

senses.label: Polite request
senses.meaning: The negative question 「〜てくださいませんか」 asks someone to do something. It is more polite than 「〜てください」 and close to 「〜ていただけませんか」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + くださいませんか／くださいますか
examples: Could you speak a little more slowly, please?
Would you sign this document, please?

notes: The masu-form is 「くださいます」 and the past is 「くださいました」. Never ✕「くださります」.
The subject (the doer) is the other person, marked with 「が」: 「先生が教えてくださった」.
「お／ご + masu-stem / kanji noun + くださる」 is even more formal, as in 「お越しくださる」 and 「ご協力くださる」.
Plain 「〜てください」 on its own is a request or instruction, not this pattern.

daily.title: Thanks for an elder's help
daily.description: Telling a friend how a teacher helped.
daily.example: My teacher actually went out of the way to call me.

daily.title: Asking for directions
daily.description: Politely asking a stranger for help.
daily.example: Excuse me, could you draw me a map?

work.title: Thanking guests in a speech
work.description: Opening an event by thanking the guests for coming.
work.example: Thank you for coming today.

work.title: Thanking a client
work.description: Thanking a client for their help in an email.
work.example: Thank you for your prompt response.

etymology: 「くださる」 was the respectful form of 「下す」 (くだす, “to bestow from above”), meaning “(a superior) grants”. As an auxiliary after a te-form, it means a superior grants the favor of an action, making it the respectful form of 「くれる」.

similar.title: 〜てくれる
similar.explanation: The plain form, used with family and friends. 「〜てくださる」 is its respectful form, used when the doer is a superior or guest.

similar.title: 〜ていただく
similar.explanation: Takes “me” as subject and is humble: 「先生に教えていただいた」. This pattern takes the other person as subject and is respectful: 「先生が教えてくださった」.

similar.title: 〜てください
similar.explanation: The imperative of 「くださる」, used for requests and instructions. It does not mean “the other person has done this for me”.

meaning: The humble form of 「〜てあげる」: my side does something for a superior or guest.
connection: Verb te-form + さしあげる (差し上げる)

senses.label: Doing for a superior
senses.meaning: The speaker's side does something for a superior, elder, or guest. It is the formal version of 「〜てあげる」. But it still implies “doing someone a favor”, so it should not be said to the person directly.
senses.connection: 目上の人に／を verb te-form + さしあげる／さしあげました
examples: I carried my teacher's bags for him.
I showed a customer the way.
I gave my seat to an elderly woman.

senses.label: Suggesting service
senses.meaning: Used when talking to a third party or when staff describe a service. When offering directly to a superior, 「お〜しましょうか」 is more appropriate.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + さしあげてください／さしあげましょう
examples: Please explain it to the customer.
Let's send the materials to the department manager.

notes: Saying ✕「先生、荷物を持ってさしあげます」 to a superior's face sounds condescending and rude. Say 「お持ちしましょうか」 instead.
It's mostly used when telling a third party, or when instructing others to help a superior or guest.
As an auxiliary verb it is usually written in kana, 「さしあげる」, but 「差し上げる」 is also possible.

daily.title: Talking about a good deed
daily.description: Telling your family you gave up your seat on the train.
daily.example: I gave my seat to an elderly person on the train.

daily.title: Showing a guest around
daily.description: Telling a friend you guided a visiting elder.
daily.example: I showed my teacher around town.

work.title: A boss instructs staff
work.description: A manager tells a team member to help a client.
work.example: Hand the client a brochure and explain it in detail.

work.title: Between store staff
work.description: A clerk reminds a coworker to look after an older customer.
work.example: Please bring that customer over there a glass of water.

etymology: 「さしあげる」 is the prefix 「差し」 + 「上げる」, originally “to hold up with both hands and offer”. It became the humble form of 「あげる」. After a te-form, it means offering an action to a superior.

similar.title: 〜てあげる
similar.explanation: The plain form, for equals and people below you. 「〜てさしあげる」 is for superiors, but both carry a sense of doing a favor.

similar.title: お〜する・ご〜する
similar.explanation: Humble patterns that only lower yourself, with no sense of doing a favor. They are the first choice when doing something for a superior face to face: 「お持ちします」, 「ご案内します」.

similar.title: 〜てやる
similar.explanation: Used toward people below you, animals, and plants. More casual than 「〜てあげる」, at the opposite end of the politeness scale from this pattern.

meaning: Doing something for someone below you, or for an animal or plant. It can also mean deliberately doing something to someone to “show them”, or a strong determination like “I'll show you I can”.
connection: Verb te-form + やる (やります／やった／やろう)

senses.label: Doing for someone below you
senses.meaning: Doing something for your own children, juniors, animals, or plants. More casual and blunt than 「〜てあげる」. Nowadays people often use 「〜てあげる」 for children and pets too.
senses.connection: Junior / animal / plant に／を verb te-form + やる
examples: I took the dog out for a walk.
I bought my son a bicycle.
I helped my little brother with his homework.

senses.label: Showing someone
senses.meaning: Deliberately doing something unpleasant or harmful to the other person. It has an aggressive, revenge-like tone. Common in arguments and lines in novels.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + やる／やった (often 「〜てやった」)
examples: He was so noisy that I yelled at him.
I'm going to get back at my mean older brother.

senses.label: Determination
senses.meaning: Shows the speaker's strong resolve or defiant feelings: “I'll show you”, “just watch me”. Often 「〜てやる」 or 「〜てやろう」, usually said to oneself.
senses.connection: Volitional verb te-form + やる／やろう (sentence-final)
examples: I'm definitely going to pass!
Someday I'll be the best in the world.

notes: In 「花に水をやる」 and 「えさをやる」, 「やる」 is the main verb “give”, not an auxiliary.
Never use it toward superiors or equals; it's very rude. Even toward juniors it can sound condescending, so in formal situations use 「〜てあげる」.
The last two meanings sound rough. They're common in casual male speech and in lines from novels and manga.

daily.title: Parents talking about their kids
daily.description: A parent tells friends what they do for their child.
daily.example: When I read my kid a picture book, he falls asleep right away.

daily.title: Reading manga
daily.description: The hero makes a vow, using 「〜てやる」 to show resolve.
daily.example: I'm going to get stronger, no matter what!

daily.title: Venting after an argument
daily.description: Complaining to a friend in a defiant tone.
daily.example: I was so mad that I told him straight out.

work.title: Chatting with coworkers about family
work.description: Coworkers talk about their weekend over lunch, a casual setting.
work.example: Over the weekend I taught my daughter how to cook.

etymology: 「やる」 (遣る) originally meant “to send, dispatch far away”, which extended to “give (to someone below, or to animals and plants)”. As an auxiliary after a te-form, it means doing an action for someone below you. From “inflicting something on someone” came the meanings “show them” and “I'll show you I can”.

similar.title: 〜てあげる
similar.explanation: More polite and gentle, and usable with equals. 「〜てやる」 is only for juniors, animals, and plants, and sounds rough. Today people often use 「〜てあげる」 for children and pets too.

similar.title: 〜てさしあげる
similar.explanation: The humble form used for superiors, the exact opposite of 「〜てやる」 on the politeness scale.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うと思う
similar.explanation: Simply states an intention. When 「〜てやる」 shows determination, it carries strong defiant, competitive feelings.

meaning: Asks someone to do something for you, softly, using a negative question: “Could you ... for me?”. More polite than 「〜てください」.
connection: Verb te-form + もらえませんか／くれませんか (casual: 〜てもらえない？／〜てくれない？)

senses.label: Could I have you...?
senses.meaning: 「〜てもらえませんか」 takes “me” as the subject. Literally, “Can't I receive ... from you?”. Polite and indirect. Used with coworkers, store staff, and strangers.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + もらえませんか／もらえますか
examples: Excuse me, could you take a picture for me?
Could you hold this bag for a moment?
Could you get back to me by tomorrow?

senses.label: Would you...?
senses.meaning: 「〜てくれませんか」 takes the other person as the subject. Literally, “Won't you ... for me?”. Slightly more direct than 「もらえませんか」, but still a polite request.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + くれませんか／くれますか
examples: Would you close the window?
Could you explain it once more?

senses.label: Casual request
senses.meaning: With friends and family, use the plain forms 「〜てくれない？」 and 「〜てもらえない？」 for a friendly tone. Say them with rising intonation.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + くれない？／もらえない？／くれる？
examples: Hey, can you pass me the salt?
Can you give me a hand?

notes: Politeness scale: 〜てくれる？ < 〜てくれない？ < 〜てくれませんか ≈ 〜てもらえませんか < 〜ていただけませんか.
A negative question 「〜ませんか」 is softer than a positive one 「〜ますか」, because it leaves room for the listener to say no.
With superiors and clients, switch to 「〜ていただけませんか」 or 「〜てくださいませんか」.

daily.title: Asking for a photo while traveling
daily.description: Asking a passerby at a tourist spot to take your picture.
daily.example: Excuse me, could you press the shutter for me?

daily.title: Asking family for help
daily.description: Asking a family member for help while cooking.
daily.example: Mom, can you taste this for me?

daily.title: On the train
daily.description: Asking the person next to you to scoot over a little.
daily.example: Excuse me, could you move over a little?

work.title: Asking a coworker for help
work.description: Asking a coworker at the same level for help.
work.example: Could you make a copy of these materials for me?

work.title: Checking a time
work.description: Discussing the meeting time with a coworker.
work.example: Could we move the meeting to three o'clock?

etymology: Built from 「もらえる」, the potential form of the auxiliary 「〜てもらう」, or from 「〜てくれる」, plus the negative question 「〜ませんか」. Making a request as a negative question is a common way in Japanese to leave the choice to the listener and sound indirect.

similar.title: 〜ていただけませんか
similar.explanation: The humble version of 「もらえませんか」. More polite, for superiors and clients.

similar.title: 〜てください
similar.explanation: A direct request or instruction, with a tone of telling the listener what to do. This pattern asks about the listener's willingness as a question, so it is more polite.

similar.title: 〜ませんか
similar.explanation: On its own, 「〜ませんか」 is an invitation to do something together (「一緒に行きませんか」), not a request to do something for me.

meaning: A very polite request for someone to do something for you: “Could you possibly ...?”. Used with superiors, clients, and strangers.
connection: Verb te-form + いただけませんか (more formal: いただけないでしょうか)

senses.label: Could you possibly...?
senses.meaning: The negative question of the potential form of 「いただく」. With “me” as subject, it literally means “Can't I humbly receive your ...?”. One of the most common polite requests.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + いただけませんか／いただけますか
examples: Could you please say that once more?
Could you tell me how to read this kanji?
Could you wait a moment, please?

senses.label: Extra-formal request
senses.meaning: 「〜ていただけないでしょうか」 is softer and more formal than 「ませんか」. Use it when the request is a big one or the listener's status is very high.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + いただけないでしょうか
examples: Would it be possible to extend the deadline by a week?
Would you be willing to write me a letter of recommendation?

notes: More polite than 「〜てもらえませんか」. It's the standard way to make requests in business.
「お／ご + masu-stem / kanji noun + いただけませんか」 is even more formal, as in 「ご確認いただけませんか」.
To ask permission to do something yourself, use 「〜させていただけませんか」.

daily.title: Asking a teacher
daily.description: A student asks the teacher a question after class.
daily.example: Could you explain this problem once more, please?

daily.title: Asking a stranger for directions
daily.description: Politely asking a stranger on the street.
daily.example: Could you tell me the way to the station?

work.title: Asking a client to check
work.description: Asking a client to confirm something by email or phone.
work.example: Sorry to trouble you, but could you check the contents?

work.title: Asking a boss for approval
work.description: Asking your boss to change a schedule.
work.example: Would it be possible to change the time of our meeting?

etymology: Built from 「いただける」, the potential form of 「〜ていただく」, plus the negative question 「〜ませんか」. Literally “Can't I receive your ...?”, it softens a request twice: once with humble language and once with a negative question.

similar.title: 〜てもらえませんか
similar.explanation: Normal politeness, used with coworkers, store staff, and so on. This pattern is its humble version and is more formal.

similar.title: 〜てくださいませんか
similar.explanation: Similar politeness. It takes the other person as subject and uses respectful language; this pattern takes “me” as subject and uses humble language. In business, this pattern is more common.

similar.title: 〜させていただけませんか
similar.explanation: Asks for permission for me to do something, so I am the doer. This pattern asks the other person to do something, so they are the doer.

meaning: Expresses that the speaker wants someone else to do (or not do) something: “I want you to ...”, “I hope ...”.
connection: (person に) verb te-form + ほしい／もらいたい; negative: verb nai-form + でほしい

senses.label: Wanting others to do
senses.meaning: Expresses a wish for someone else to do something. The one who wishes is the speaker; the doer is someone else, marked with 「に」. It can also express a wish for something to happen (「早く春が来てほしい」).
senses.connection: Person に verb te-form + ほしい／ほしかった
examples: I want my mother to live a long life.
I hope the rain stops soon.
I'd like you to help me with this job.

senses.label: Wanting others not to do
senses.meaning: 「〜ないでほしい」 means you'd like the other person not to do something. It is softer than 「〜ないでください」 and conveys the speaker's feelings.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + でほしい
examples: I'd rather you didn't smoke here.
I'd like you not to tell anyone about this.

senses.label: Wanting help
senses.meaning: 「〜てもらいたい」 is 「〜てもらう」 + 「たい」. It means basically the same as 「〜てほしい」, but sounds a little more formal. The polite version is 「〜ていただきたい」.
senses.connection: Person に verb te-form + もらいたい／いただきたい
examples: I'd like you to submit this document by the end of today.
I'd really like you to take a look at it sometime.

notes: 「〜てほしい」 expresses the speaker's own wish. For a third person's wish, use 「〜てほしがっている」 or 「〜てほしいそうだ」.
Saying 「〜てほしいです」 directly to a superior sounds pushy. Use a request form such as 「〜ていただけませんか」 instead.
「noun + がほしい」 means wanting a thing; 「〜てほしい」 means wanting someone to do something. Keep them apart.

daily.title: A wish for family
daily.description: Telling a family member how you feel.
daily.example: I wish you'd come home a bit earlier.

daily.title: A reminder to a friend
daily.description: Asking a friend not to do something.
daily.example: I'm worried, so please don't push yourself too hard.

daily.title: Hoping for good weather
daily.description: Hoping for sunshine before an outing.
daily.example: I hope it's sunny tomorrow.

work.title: A boss's expectations
work.description: A manager sets expectations in a meeting.
work.example: I want all of you to achieve this goal.

work.title: Expressing a wish to a client
work.description: Using a formal expression to state a hope.
work.example: We would very much like you to try our new product.

etymology: 「ほしい」 (欲しい) is an adjective meaning “wanted, desired”. After a te-form, what is wanted expands from a thing to someone else's action. 「〜てもらいたい」 combines the auxiliary 「もらう」 with the wish ending 「たい」.

similar.title: 〜たい
similar.explanation: 「〜たい」 is wanting to do something yourself; 「〜てほしい」 is wanting someone else to do it. 「行きたい」 = I want to go; 「行ってほしい」 = I want you to go.

similar.title: 〜がほしい
similar.explanation: Wanting a thing: 「車がほしい」. This pattern wants someone else's action.

similar.title: 〜てもらえませんか
similar.explanation: This pattern states your own wish; 「〜てもらえませんか」 is a direct request to the listener.

meaning: Causative form + a giving/receiving verb. Asks for permission to do something yourself, or humbly says “allow me to ...”.
connection: Causative te-form (〜させて／〜せて) + ください／もらう／いただく

senses.label: Let me do it
senses.meaning: 「〜させてください」 directly asks the listener to let you do something. It shows an eager, proactive attitude.
senses.connection: Causative te-form + ください
examples: Please let me handle that job.
Let me think about it for a bit.
I'm not feeling well, so please let me go home early.

senses.label: Being allowed to do
senses.meaning: 「〜させてもらう」 means you did something after getting the other person's permission (or kindness). It carries thanks. 「〜させてもらえませんか」 politely asks for permission.
senses.connection: Causative te-form + もらう／もらえませんか
examples: My friend let me stay at his place for a night.
Could I use your restroom for a moment?

senses.label: Doing it humbly
senses.meaning: 「〜させていただく」 is humble language: “allow me to ...”. It is often used to formally announce your own action, as in speeches and notices.
senses.connection: Causative te-form + いただきます／いただけませんか
examples: Well then, allow me to begin my presentation.
We are closed today.
May I explain this matter briefly?

notes: Causative forms: ichidan 「食べる→食べさせる」; godan 「やる→やらせる」; 「する→させる」, 「来る→来させる」.
「〜させていただく」 is overused these days, even when no permission is needed, and some people find it wordy, as in 「この度結婚させていただきました」.
Don't confuse it with 「見せてください」 (please show me) or 「知らせてください」 (please let me know). These are ordinary verbs, not causatives.

daily.title: Offering to take care of something
daily.description: Volunteering at a get-together with friends.
daily.example: Let me pay for dinner today.

daily.title: Asking parents
daily.description: A child asks parents for permission.
daily.example: Please, let me go study abroad.

work.title: Speaking at a meeting
work.description: Formally starting to speak at a meeting.
work.example: Well then, allow me to introduce myself.

work.title: Asking the boss for a day off
work.description: Asking a manager for time off.
work.example: Would it be possible for me to take next Friday off?

work.title: A store notice
work.description: A sign announcing a temporary closure.
work.example: We apologize for the inconvenience, but we will be temporarily closed.

etymology: Made from the causative 「〜させる」 (make/let someone do) + the giving/receiving auxiliaries 「くれる」 (imperative 「ください」), 「もらう」, and 「いただく」. Literally, “please give me the favor of letting me do it”, that is, “please allow me to do it”.

similar.title: 〜せる・〜させる (causative)
similar.explanation: The causative alone means making or letting someone else do something, so the other person is the doer. In this pattern “I” am the doer, asking permission to act.

similar.title: 〜てもいいですか
similar.explanation: Also asks for permission, but simply asks “is it OK?”. 「〜させてください」 carries a strong, eager “please let me do it”.

similar.title: 〜ていただけませんか
similar.explanation: Asks the other person to do something for me, so they are the doer. 「〜させていただけませんか」 asks them to let me do it, so I am the doer.

title: 〜させられる (causative-passive)
meaning: Combines the causative and the passive. It means being made to do something you don't want to do. It can also mean that something stirred your feelings or thoughts.
connection: Ichidan verbs, する, 来る: 〜させられる; godan verbs: 〜せられる／〜される (short form)

senses.label: Being made to do
senses.meaning: The subject is the person forced to act; the one forcing is marked with 「に」. It means “to be made to do something against one's will”, with a tone of suffering or complaint.
senses.connection: Person に causative-passive verb (食べさせられる／行かされる／させられる)
examples: As a kid, my mother made me eat vegetables I hated.
An older coworker made me drink.
I was kept waiting at the station for a whole hour.

senses.label: Can't help feeling
senses.meaning: Something makes the subject naturally feel or think something. Often used with 「考える」, 「感動する」, 「驚く」, and 「反省する」. There is no complaint about being forced.
senses.connection: 「考えさせられる」, 「感動させられる」, 「驚かされる」, etc.
examples: This movie really made me think about a lot of things.
His hard work is truly amazing.

notes: Godan verbs often use the short form: 行かせられる→行かされる, 待たせられる→待たされる. But verbs ending in 「す」 cannot be shortened: 「話す」→✕「話さされる」; only 「話させられる」 is correct.
How to build it: 書く → causative 「書かせる」 → passive 「書かせられる」 (short: 「書かされる」).
The subject is the person who is forced; the one forcing takes 「に」: 「私は母に掃除をさせられた」.

daily.title: Complaining to a friend
daily.description: Friends complaining about being made to do things by their parents.
daily.example: Yesterday I was made to clean my room all day.

daily.title: Remembering school days
daily.description: Talking about how tough your club activities were.
daily.example: In my club, they made us run ten laps around the field every day.

daily.title: After a documentary
daily.description: Talking about being deeply moved by a work.
daily.example: That documentary really made you think, didn't it?

work.title: Complaining about overtime
work.description: Coworkers privately complain about forced overtime.
work.example: The section chief made me work overtime again.

work.title: An evaluation in a report
work.description: News or commentary describing something thought-provoking.
work.example: This accident makes us think again about how important safety management is.

etymology: Formed by stacking the causative auxiliary 「せる・させる」 and the passive auxiliary 「られる」: 「させ + られる」. The godan short form 「〜される」 comes from simplifying the 「せら」 in 「〜せられる」, and it is more common in speech.

similar.title: 〜せる・〜させる (causative)
similar.explanation: The causative takes the one forcing as subject: 「母が私に野菜を食べさせた」. The causative-passive takes the one forced as subject: 「私は母に野菜を食べさせられた」.

similar.title: 〜れる・〜られる (passive)
similar.explanation: The passive only means receiving someone's action: 「母に叱られた」. The causative-passive means being made by someone to do something yourself.

similar.title: 〜させてください
similar.explanation: Also a causative form plus something else, but it means “please let me do it”, an eager wish, the exact opposite of being forced.

title: 〜られる・〜える (potential form)
meaning: The potential form of verbs. It means being able to do something, or that something is possible under certain conditions.
connection: Godan verbs: change the final u-row sound to the e-row + る (書く→書ける); ichidan verbs: 〜られる (食べる→食べられる); 来る→来られる; する→できる

senses.label: Ability
senses.meaning: The subject has the ability to do something. The object is usually marked with 「が」, though 「を」 is also possible. Like “can” or “know how to”.
senses.connection: Noun が godan verb e-row + る (泳げる・話せる・読める)
examples: I can speak a little Japanese.
My little brother can't swim yet.
Can you read this kanji?

senses.label: Possible under conditions
senses.meaning: Something is possible in a certain situation or under certain conditions. It has nothing to do with personal ability; it depends on outside circumstances.
senses.connection: Ichidan verb 〜られる (食べられる・来られる・見られる)／godan verb e-row + る
examples: Is this water drinkable?
Can you come to the party tomorrow?
You can take photos of Mt. Fuji from here.

senses.label: ら-dropping (ら抜き言葉)
senses.meaning: In casual speech, ichidan verbs and 「来る」 often drop the 「ら」: 「見れる」, 「食べれる」, 「来れる」. Very common in conversation, but use 「〜られる」 in formal writing and on tests.
senses.connection: Ichidan verb 〜れる (casual): 見れる・食べれる・寝れる
examples: I couldn't sleep much last night.
Can you come tomorrow?
You can watch this movie online.

notes: For ichidan verbs, the potential 「〜られる」 looks the same as the passive and honorific forms. Context decides: 「食べられる」 can mean “can eat” or “be eaten”.
The potential form of 「する」 is 「できる」. 「〜ことができる」 is a more formal, written way to say it.
「見える」 and 「聞こえる」 mean something is naturally visible or audible; 「見られる」 and 「聞ける」 mean you have the chance or conditions to see or hear it.
Potential forms are ichidan verbs and conjugate like them: 書ける→書けない→書けます.

daily.title: Introducing yourself
daily.description: Talking about your skills.
daily.example: I can play the guitar a little.

daily.title: Ordering food
daily.description: Asking whether someone can eat something.
daily.example: Can you eat spicy food?

daily.title: Making plans with a friend
daily.description: Checking whether a friend can come.
daily.example: What time can you come on Saturday?

work.title: Confirming a shipping date
work.description: Checking with a client whether something can be sent in time.
work.example: Can you send it by Friday?

work.title: Explaining a service
work.description: Explaining a system's features to a client.
work.example: You can view your past statements in this app.

etymology: The ichidan 「られる」 comes from the classical auxiliary 「らる」, which once covered four meanings: spontaneous, potential, passive, and honorific. Godan potential forms (書ける, etc.) developed after the Edo period by simplifying forms like 「書かれる」, and became independent “potential verbs”. 「ら抜き」 is ichidan verbs changing by analogy with the godan potential verbs.

similar.title: 〜ことができる
similar.explanation: Same meaning, but more formal and written. The potential form is shorter and more conversational.

similar.title: 〜が見える・〜が聞こえる
similar.explanation: 「見える」 means something naturally comes into view; 「見られる」 means having the conditions or chance to see it. 「星が見える」, 「この映画はネットで見られる」.

similar.title: 〜れる・〜られる (passive)
similar.explanation: For ichidan verbs, the potential and passive forms look the same. For godan verbs they differ: passive 「書かれる」, potential 「書ける」.

meaning: A sight or sound naturally reaches your eyes or ears, with no effort on your part: “can be seen”, “can be heard”.
connection: Noun + が + 見える／聞こえる

senses.label: Can be seen
senses.meaning: 「見える」 means something naturally comes into view. The object takes 「が」. It's an intransitive verb, outside the person's control.
senses.connection: Noun が 見える (見えます／見えない)
examples: You can see Mt. Fuji from the window.
It's so dark I can't see anything.
Without my glasses, I can't see well.

senses.label: Can be heard
senses.meaning: 「聞こえる」 means a sound naturally reaches your ears. The object takes 「が」. It is also outside your control.
senses.connection: Noun が 聞こえる (聞こえます／聞こえない)
examples: I can hear music from the next room.
Sorry, I can't hear you very well.
I heard birds singing in the distance.

notes: 「見える」 and 「聞こえる」 mean seeing and hearing naturally; 「見られる」 and 「聞ける」 mean being able to see or hear under certain conditions. To describe the view in front of you, say 「窓から海が見える」, not 「海が見られる」.
「〜に見える」 and 「〜く見える」 mean “look like ...”, and 「〜に聞こえる」 means “sound like ...”. That's a different use.
「お見えになる」 is the respectful form of 「来る」 and has nothing to do with seeing.

daily.title: Describing the view from your room
daily.description: Telling a friend about the view from your new home.
daily.example: You can see the ocean from this room.

daily.title: A bad phone connection
daily.description: The voice keeps cutting out on a call.
daily.example: Hello? Can you hear me?

daily.title: A night walk
daily.description: Looking at the stars with family.
daily.example: You can see lots of stars tonight.

work.title: An online meeting
work.description: Before starting, checking whether everyone can hear and see.
work.example: Can everyone hear me? Can you see my screen?

work.title: Introducing a hotel room
work.description: Hotel staff describe the room to a guest.
work.example: You can see Tokyo Tower from this room.

etymology: 「見える」 comes from 「見る」 plus the classical spontaneous auxiliary 「ゆ」 (見ゆ→見える), meaning “to come into view naturally”. 「聞こえる」 likewise comes from 「聞く」 + 「ゆ」 (聞こゆ→聞こえる). So both naturally carry the idea of “happening on its own, not by will”.

similar.title: 見られる・聞ける (potential form)
similar.explanation: The potential form stresses having the conditions or chance to see or hear: 「このサイトで映画が見られる」, 「ラジオでニュースが聞ける」.

similar.title: 〜く見える・〜に見える
similar.explanation: Means “look ...”, a judgment about appearance: 「若く見える」, 「元気に見える」. Not “can be seen”.

similar.title: 見る・聞く
similar.explanation: 「見る」 and 「聞く」 are deliberate looking and listening. They are transitive verbs, and the object takes 「を」: 「テレビを見る」, 「音楽を聞く」.

meaning: A respectful pattern that describes the actions of the listener or a superior more respectfully, raising the doer.
connection: お + verb masu-stem + になる; ご + kanji action noun + になる

senses.label: Native Japanese verbs
senses.meaning: Shows respect for the actions of superiors and guests. The subject is the other person. More respectful than 「〜れる・〜られる」.
senses.connection: お + verb masu-stem + になる (お読みになる・お帰りになる・お待ちになる)
examples: The president has already gone home.
Have you read this book, professor?
Please, go ahead and use this seat.

senses.label: Kanji nouns
senses.meaning: Put 「ご」 before a kanji action noun. Common examples are 「ご覧になる」 (see), 「ご利用になる」 (use), and 「ご出席になる」 (attend).
senses.connection: ご + kanji noun + になる (ご覧になる・ご利用になる)
examples: Did you see yesterday's news?
This card can be used at our stores nationwide.

notes: Verbs that have their own special respectful form don't use this pattern: ✕お見になる→ご覧になる; ✕お行きになる→いらっしゃる; ✕お言いになる→おっしゃる.
Verbs whose masu-stem is only one syllable (見る, 寝る, いる, etc.) can't use it: ✕お見になる, ✕お寝になる.
「お〜になれる」 is the potential form, “you can ...”, common in explanations and notices.
In 「お世話になる」 and 「ご迷惑になる」, 「〜になる」 means “become”. They are not this pattern.

daily.title: Talking with a teacher
daily.description: A student asks a teacher a question.
daily.example: Around what time will you be back, professor?

daily.title: Speaking to an elder
daily.description: Asking a friend's parent something when greeting them.
daily.example: Has your father already gone to bed?

work.title: Receiving a client
work.description: The receptionist checks with a client.
work.example: Mr. Yamada, around what time will you arrive?

work.title: Explaining a product
work.description: Explaining to customers how to use a product.
work.example: This service is available to members only.

work.title: Relaying the boss's whereabouts
work.description: Telling a caller that the manager is out.
work.example: The department manager is out at a meeting right now.

etymology: 「お」 is a respectful prefix (from 「御 (おほみ)」), and 「になる」 originally means “to become”. Literally, “(your action) naturally becomes ...”. Instead of saying the other person “does” something directly, it uses this indirect “becoming” to show respect.

similar.title: 〜れる・〜られる (respectful)
similar.explanation: Also respectful language, but lighter, often used in writing and news. 「お〜になる」 shows more respect and is common in speech.

similar.title: お〜する・ご〜する (humble)
similar.explanation: Looks similar but points the opposite way: 「お〜する」 is my own action, lowering myself (「お持ちします」); 「お〜になる」 is the other person's action, raising them (「お持ちになる」).

similar.title: いらっしゃる・おっしゃる
similar.explanation: If a verb has a special respectful form, use that instead of 「お〜になる」.

meaning: The respectful version of 「〜てください」, politely asking someone to do something. Common in customer service, announcements, and notices.
connection: お + verb masu-stem + ください; ご + kanji action noun + ください

senses.label: Native Japanese verbs
senses.meaning: Uses respectful language to request or instruct. More polite than 「〜てください」. Common from store staff, in station announcements, and in business.
senses.connection: お + verb masu-stem + ください (お待ちください・お入りください)
examples: Please wait a moment.
Please, come in.
Please feel free to contact us.

senses.label: Kanji nouns
senses.meaning: Put 「ご」 before a kanji action noun. Common for reminders and requests in notices, emails, and announcements.
senses.connection: ご + kanji noun + ください (ご注意ください・ご確認ください)
examples: Please watch your step.
For details, please see our website.
Please check the contents.

notes: An even more formal version is 「お〜くださいませ」, often heard in stores and hotels.
If a verb has a special respectful form, use it: ✕お見ください→ご覧ください; ✕お来ください→お越しください／いらしてください.
It's still an imperative. When asking a superior face to face, a question like 「お〜いただけますか」 sounds softer.

daily.title: Shopping in a store
daily.description: A clerk asks a customer to wait.
daily.example: I'll bring it right away, so please wait here.

daily.title: A station announcement
daily.description: An announcement reminding passengers to stay safe.
daily.example: Please stand behind the yellow line.

daily.title: Making a guest comfortable
daily.description: A host welcomes a visitor.
daily.example: Please, have a seat.

work.title: A business email
work.description: At the end of an email, asking the reader to check an attachment.
work.example: Please check the attached materials.

work.title: A meeting notice
work.description: Telling attendees what to note before a meeting.
work.example: Please read the meeting materials in advance.

etymology: Made from the respectful prefix 「お／ご」 + the verb's masu-stem (used as a noun) + 「ください」, the imperative of 「くださる」. Literally, “please grant me your ...”. Turning the action into a noun avoids a direct command and shows respect.

similar.title: 〜てください
similar.explanation: An ordinary request or instruction, with less respect. 「待ってください」 → the more polite 「お待ちください」.

similar.title: お〜になる
similar.explanation: Also a respectful pattern, but used to describe the other person's actions; 「お〜ください」 is used to ask them to do something.

similar.title: 〜ていただけませんか
similar.explanation: A request in question form that leaves the choice to the listener, so it's softer than 「お〜ください」.
